Introduction and meaning
Hurt = bodily pain, disease or infirmity (old 319). Definition only; punishment is s. 115. BNS restatement of IPC 319. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 114 is the rule on “Hurt”. The section provides that whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 114 exists so that “Hurt” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
114. Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt

hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 114 (Hurt), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 114 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 114 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

Comprehensive Written Submissions. Deepen the doctrinal synthesis with four foundational layers.

Layer 1 — Place the section in the Chapter. Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.. Show why this heading sits where it sits.

Layer 2 — Work a second, slightly harder hypothetical. Change one ingredient and show why the section then fails.

learningObjectives: Master the tripartite definition of hurt under BNS s. 114: bodily pain, disease, or infirmity.
Understand the minimal threshold required to constitute hurt in criminal law.
Distinguish hurt from assault, criminal force, and grievous hurt.
Analyze the absence of external marks as a factor in establishing bodily pain.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 114 defines hurt as causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Criminalizes any unauthorized non-consensual physical interference that produces bodily pain, causes disease, or impairs the physiological function of another human being.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 114 (corresponding to IPC s. 319).
Three independent statutory modalities: (1) Bodily pain; (2) Disease; (3) Infirmity.
Relationship with subsequent sections: Section 114 provides the base definition; Section 115 penalizes voluntarily causing hurt; Section 116 elevates it to grievous hurt.
essentialIngredients: The victim suffered bodily pain; OR
The victim contracted a disease as a result of the accused's act; OR
The victim suffered bodily infirmity (temporary or permanent functional impairment).
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 114 provides the foundational definition of physical harm. The law recognizes three distinct forms of hurt. First, 'bodily pain' covers any physical sensation of pain, even if of short duration and leaving no external bruises, cuts, or visible marks (e.g., pulling hair, slapping, twisting an arm). Second, 'disease' covers transmitting or causing an infectious or debilitating illness (e.g., deliberately contaminating food or water with cholera or communicable pathogens). Third, 'infirmity' means the temporary or permanent impairment of any organ or mental faculty (e.g., rendering someone unconscious by administering a tranquilizer, or causing temporary paralysis). Hurt is purely physical or physiological; mere emotional distress or mental anguish without bodily suffering does not fall under Section 114.
examples: Teaching example (Bodily pain without marks): An accused slaps a colleague across the face with significant force, causing acute pain that stings for several hours, but leaves no visible redness or laceration. This satisfies 'bodily pain' under s. 114.

Teaching example (Infirmity via drugs): An accused slips a sleep-inducing chemical into a roommate's drink, causing the roommate to collapse into unconsciousness for eight hours. This temporary impairment of bodily faculties constitutes 'infirmity'.
distinctions: Hurt (s. 114) vs Grievous Hurt (s. 116): Hurt covers any bodily pain, disease, or infirmity; Grievous Hurt is strictly confined to the eight severe statutory categories under Section 116.
Hurt (s. 114) vs Assault (s. 130): Assault is the gesture or preparation causing apprehension of force; Hurt is the actual physical harm or pain caused.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who intentionally twisted a victim's fingers backwards, causing severe pain for several days but no fracture or dislocation, caused hurt.
Rule: Under BNS s. 114, causing bodily pain constitutes hurt.
Application: Severe pain was intentionally inflicted, satisfying the bodily pain requirement.
Conclusion: The act constitutes hurt under BNS s. 114.
